chapter.title: When the path gets rough

cards.body:
Halfway up a trail, someone behind you shouts, 'Wait, why this way?' A good guide doesn't freeze, and doesn't sprint ahead either: **they stop, plant their feet, and point**.

Answering on the spot like that is a skill you can practise. You don't have to be born with it.
cards.simpler: Picture yourself halfway up a trail. Someone behind you shouts, 'Wait, why this way?' A good guide doesn't freeze. A good guide doesn't rush ahead either. **They stop, plant their feet, and point**. Answering a question on the spot is a skill you can practise. You don't need to be born with it.

cards.prompt: You're leading six friends up a hill. Near the top, Jo asks, 'Why didn't we just take the cable car?' Everyone stops walking. What should you do first?

options.text: Answer straight away, before the silence gets awkward
Pause for two seconds, then give a short answer that ends with a direction

whyNot.a: That's filling the silence, not answering it. A rushed reply tends to wander because you haven't picked a shape yet.
whyNot.c: That's dodging, not guiding. Jo still doesn't know why, and now the whole group is wondering too.

cards.reteach: A surprise question feels like an emergency, but it isn't one. A short pause looks like thinking to everyone watching. Then a good answer ends by pointing somewhere, the way a guide's arm points to the next turn.

cards.title: Pause, then three steps
cards.body:
When a question catches you off guard, you'll want to fill the silence fast. Don't. You'd think a pause looks weak. To the room, two seconds of quiet looks like someone taking the question seriously.

Then answer in three short steps, a shape taught by Matt Abrahams, who teaches at Stanford. *What*: your answer, in one sentence. *So what*: why it matters to them. *Now what*: the next step. **Pause, then What, So what, Now what.**

It's a guide at a fork in the trail: that peak, it's worth it for the view, we go left at the big rock.
cards.simpler: When a question surprises you, you'll want to fill the quiet fast. Don't. Two seconds of quiet doesn't look weak. It looks like you're taking it seriously. Then answer in three short steps, from Matt Abrahams, who teaches at Stanford. What: your answer, in one sentence. So what: why it matters to them. Now what: the next step. **Pause, then What, So what, Now what.** A guide at a fork says: that peak, worth it for the view, left at the big rock.

cards.title: The umbrella question
cards.body:
Dev gives a 5-minute talk at work pitching a cycle-to-work scheme. At the end, a colleague holding a dripping umbrella asks, 'What happens when it rains?'

Dev pauses, counts to two silently, then answers. *What:* 'You change at work: there are lockers and a drying rail on floor 2.' *So what:* 'Rain is a big reason people stop cycling, so this is what keeps the scheme alive past November.' *Now what:* 'Try it for one wet week.'

That took forty seconds. The umbrella's owner signed up.
cards.simpler: Dev gives a five-minute talk at work pitching a cycle-to-work scheme. At the end, a colleague with a dripping umbrella asks, 'What happens when it rains?' Dev **pauses for two silent seconds**, then answers. What: 'You change at work: there are lockers and a drying rail on floor 2.' So what: 'Rain is a big reason people stop cycling, so this is what keeps the scheme alive past November.' Now what: 'Try it for one wet week.' Forty seconds. The umbrella's owner signed up.

cards.prompt: At your book club you've just recommended a novel. Someone asks, 'Isn't it far too long?' Which answer uses the idea?

options.text: 'Ha, yes, sorry, it is long. Anyway, the cover is lovely, and...'
(two-second pause) 'It is long, about 600 pages. But the chapters are short, so one fits a bus ride. Read the first three this week and decide.'
'Great question. Length is fascinating. Tolstoy also wrote long books, and in Russia at the time...'

whyNot.a: That's an apology, not an answer. There's no So what and no Now what, and it trails off.
whyNot.c: That's a ramble, not a path. It never says why this matters to them or what to do next.

cards.reteach: Check each answer against three boxes. Does it give the point in one sentence? Does it say why the listener should care? Does it end with a next step? Only one option ticks all three.

cards.title: Before you start
cards.body:
Nerves are your body packing for a climb: a fast heart, a dry mouth, shaky hands.

In the minute before you speak, standing by the projector, **breathe out slower than you breathe in**: in for a count of four, out for a count of six. Do it three times, and feel both feet flat on the floor.
cards.simpler: Nerves are your body getting ready for a climb: fast heart, dry mouth, shaky hands. In the minute before you speak, standing by the projector, **breathe out slower than you breathe in**: in for a count of four, out for a count of six. Do it three times, feet flat on the floor.

cards.body:
Sam is asked, 'Have you thought about the budget?' Sam says 'basically' three times, circles back to slide 4, and finishes four minutes later with '...so, yeah.' Nobody knows where the trail went.

How to spot it: if you can't hear your own ending coming, you skipped *Now what*, the step that tells people where to walk next.
cards.simpler: Someone asks Sam, 'Have you thought about the budget?' Sam says 'basically' three times, goes back to slide 4, and ends four minutes later with '...so, yeah.' Nobody knows where the trail went. Here's how to spot it. If you can't hear your own ending coming, **you skipped Now what**, the step that tells people where to walk next.

cards.prompt: Lena is asked why the team should switch to the new rota. She says, 'It gives everyone one free Friday a month. That means fewer people burn out over winter.' Then she stops. Which step did she skip?

whyNot.a: That's the step she got right, not the gap: 'one free Friday a month' is her answer in one sentence.
whyNot.b: That's there, not missing: 'fewer people burn out' is why it matters to them.

cards.reteach: Line the answer up against the three steps. What is the answer itself, So what is why they should care, and Now what is the next move. Lena gave the first two and left the team standing at the fork.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
When a question surprises you, **stop for two seconds, then answer in three steps**: what you think, why it matters to them, and what happens next. Before you speak, breathe out slowly.

Be the guide on the trail: stop, plant your feet, point the way.
cards.simpler: When a question surprises you, **stop for two seconds, then answer in three steps**: what you think, why it matters to them, and what happens next. Before you speak, breathe out slowly. Be the guide on the trail: stop, plant your feet, point the way.

cards.body:
Tonight, ask someone at home to throw one random question at you, like 'Best meal of your life?' Pause for two seconds, then answer with What, So what, Now what. Time it. Aim for under a minute.

Tomorrow: why your last slide should never say 'thank you'.
cards.simpler: Tonight, ask someone at home to throw one random question at you, like 'Best meal of your life?' **Pause for two seconds**, then answer in three steps: What, So what, Now what. Time yourself while you do it. Try to finish in under a minute. Tomorrow: why your last slide should never say 'thank you'.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now answer a question you didn't expect in under a minute, with a clear beginning, middle and end.

dubious_claims: Minor issue: Dev's 'What' line ('Rain is the real reason people stop cycling') doesn't actually answer 'What happens when it rains?', so the example models the What step weakly. Matt Abrahams teaching at Stanford and the What/So what/Now what structure are both accurate.
repairedFrom.why: Card 6 crams three new ideas into one card (breathing, asking what a fuzzy question means, waiting after you ask the room something), no exercise tests any of them, and the final 'In one breath' teach card has no concrete image.
repairedFrom.fix: Cut card 6 down to the breathing tip with one physical moment (e.g. 'standing by the projector, breathe out for a count of six'). Move the fuzzy-question and wait-for-the-room tips to a later chapter, and move the 'Tomorrow: thank-you slide' teaser after the try card so it's the chapter's last line.
